problem_motivation.content: There is a gap in research regarding the mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn HEA compared to its corrosion resistance.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: However, current research on the FeNiCrMn HEA has primarily focused on its corrosion resistance, with relatively limited studies on its mechanical properties.

problem_motivation.content: There is currently a lack of theoretical research on the dynamic loading behavior of FeNiCrMn HEAs at different temperatures and strain rates.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: However, there is currently a lack of theoretical research on the dynamic loading behavior of this alloy at different temperatures and strain rates.

prior_approach.content: Wu et al. reported that excluding Co results in mechanical properties similar to or better than the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Wu et al. [ [10] ] reported that when Co is excluded, the mechanical properties of FeNiMnCr18 are similar to or even better than those of the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA.

prior_approach.content: Qi et al. used MD simulations to analyze plastic deformation in CoCrFeMnNi HEAs, observing phenomena like phase transformation and twinning.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Qi et al. [ [14] ] analyzed the plastic deformation of single-crystal and polycrystalline CoCrFeMnNi HEAs under tension and compression using MD simulations.

causal_claim.content: Yielding is caused by the generation of dislocations, evidenced by a sudden stress drop.
causal_claim.evidence_span: yielding occurred, accompanied by a sudden drop in stress, which was attributed to the generation of dislocations.

causal_claim.content: Higher strain rates lead to higher dislocation densities during tensile loading.
causal_claim.evidence_span: During tensile loading, higher strain rates led to higher dislocation densities.

causal_claim.content: Increasing temperature reduces yield strength and yield strain by intensifying atomic thermal vibrations and reducing critical resolved shear stress.
causal_claim.evidence_span: At a constant strain rate, the yield strength of the alloy exhibited a decreasing trend as the temperature increased

causal_claim.content: Higher strain rates lead to higher dislocation densities and elevated flow stress due to insufficient time for dislocation annihilation.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Higher strain rates correspond to instantaneous dislocation density strengthening, which leads to higher flow stress

mechanism_principle.content: The decrease in yield strength at elevated temperatures is due to intensified atomic vibrations facilitating dislocation nucleation.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: Elevated temperatures intensify atomic thermal vibrations, making it easier for atoms to deviate from their equilibrium positions and facilitating dislocation nucleation and movement.

mechanism_principle.content: Higher strain rates result in greater deformation in a shorter time, increasing local stress which drives dislocation activation, while preventing sufficient time for annihilation or cross-slip.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: This was mainly because a higher strain rate means that the material undergoes a greater amount of deformation in a shorter time, resulting in increased local internal stress. This provides the driving force for dislocations to overcome energy barriers and activate more slip systems, leading to increased dislocation density. At lower strain rates, dislocations have sufficient time to move and interact—such as annihilating or rearranging through cross-slip or climb—which helps reduce the dislocation density. However, at higher strain rates, dislocation motion and interaction may not keep pace with the deformation process, resulting in more dislocation accumulation and insufficient annihilation

contradiction.content: The study found that yield strength is insensitive to strain rate, contrasting with previous studies which suggested that increasing strain rate restricts dislocation motion and enhances yield strength.
contradiction.evidence_span: Previous studies have shown that increasing the strain rate can restrict dislocation motion, thereby enhancing the yield strength of materials. However, in this study, the strain rate had a negligible effect on the mechanical properties of the alloy.
